manifest.description: A design critique you can run before you ask a colleague. Give it one screenshot, a whole multi-screen flow, a Figma file, a git repo, or a URL that is already serving, and it finds the candidate screens, lets you choose what to look at, then reports back the way an experienced designer would: an overall read, what is working, and the things worth tightening, each tied to a named heuristic. Multi-screen flows also get cross-screen findings that a single screen cannot show — inconsistent controls, missing progress, no way back, dead ends. It renders code and Figma before judging them, so it never critiques visuals it has not actually seen, and it says plainly which screens it could not get to instead of guessing.
manifest.highlight_1: Takes screenshots, a Figma link, a git repo, a local folder, or a running URL — and says back what it found before it starts
manifest.highlight_2: Measures contrast and hit-target sizes from the rendered page rather than estimating them from an image
manifest.highlight_3: Multi-screen flows get cross-screen checks: control consistency, progress, a way back, repeated asks, dead ends
manifest.highlight_4: Every finding names the heuristic behind it (Nielsen 1-10, WCAG, Gestalt, Fitts) and carries a severity on the NN/g 1-4 scale
manifest.highlight_5: Select any line of the report and ask a follow-up question about it, in place
manifest.highlight_6: Tells you what it could not see instead of critiquing a blank or blocked screen
manifest.highlight_7: Hands off the work it reviews: it never installs that project's dependencies, runs its scripts, starts its dev server, or edits its files
manifest.highlight_8: To take pictures it uses a headless browser, downloaded once into a cache in your home directory on first use and never into the project
manifest.use_case_1: Critique one screen or a complete product flow with severity-ranked, heuristic-backed findings tied to visible regions.
manifest.configuration_1: Drop in screenshots for zero-setup review, or provide a Figma file, repository, local folder, or already-running URL; private GitHub sources may require gh auth login.
